doc.title: Toshiko Akiyoshi interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 17, 1999

chapter: Finding her voice as a composer
title: Turning to writing and the start of the Los Angeles band
summary: The 1967 Town Hall concert showed her she wanted to write; in 1972 Lew's Tonight Show job led to Wednesday rehearsals in Los Angeles.

story.theme_name: Going west: California and the Los Angeles scene
story.community_name: Going west: moving to and working in California

blocks.x: became interested in writing much, much later, perhaps ’67, around there. Actually in ’67 I had my own concert, my own produced, to try and get money for work and so on, at the Town Hall and at that time I thought, I was hoping that if some people noticed me, and I had a solo and trio, and about four big band charts. And when I was rehearsing that I felt that’s what I wanted to do. I felt like that’s what I wanted to do. Because up to that point I was getting a little bit of anxiety about the fact that, as you know I had a quartet at one time with Mariano and so on, but it wasn’t enough color for me. I said I needed more color. So I had this anxiety, I couldn’t fully express my thoughts so to speak. So when I did that I felt like oh that’s what I’d like to do. I think that’s what I feel very comfortable wanting about — I always played and I always said afterward, why did I do that? I shouldn’t have done that. And while I’m playing I said oh I did it again. I didn’t think I ever would have said oh my God I did it again. So writing is something you can take your time, if you don’t like it you can change, so on, so on. So I think that’s maybe one part of it and if I were painting I’d probably need a lot of color. I think that’s probably it. But I couldn’t really do it. I didn’t have the money, so it was a rehearsal band so to speak, until 1972, we moved to, because of Lew’s job with the Tonight Show, he went to Los Angeles and out from boredom he remembered that I had four charts, so he suggested he would get the musicians together and we rehearsed every Wednesday morning from 10:15. Fifty cents for two hours. The union had a rehearsal and still do, I think it’s $5 now, but in those days it was fifty cents for two and half hours or something like that. So that’s how it started. And people wanted to hear and so on and so on. But I never wanted, I still don’t, as a rule I’m not interested in big bands.

That’s an interesting statement. I mean you certainly made an impact and kept that tradition alive. You know when you read about your music, most people mention that it brings in a whole other area of influence from your native culture. And when you write do you consciously try to think of things from your youth that are now combined with American jazz, or is it just kind of part of you?
